topic.title: Stratified sampling and estimating populations from samples
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: A 3- to 4-mark stratified part in most series, usually the last part of a bigger statistics question (Summer 2023 Q18, Summer 2025 Q22(c), November 2025 Q23(c), Summer 2026 Q20), plus a 4- to 5-mark population-estimate-and-critique question in some (Summer 2024 Q15). The hardest versions take the sample from a subgroup, or from frequencies that must first be read off a histogram.
mustMemorise: Stratum share of the sample = (stratum size ÷ population) × sample size
When the sample is taken from a subgroup, that subgroup's total is the population for the calculation
Answers are whole people, animals or objects; round, and check the parts add to the sample size
If the rounded parts fall short, the extra place goes to the group whose exact value had the largest fractional part
Population estimate: (marked in the second sample ÷ size of that sample) = (number marked ÷ population)
Part of a class = (width of the part ÷ width of the class) × frequency, assuming an even spread
On a histogram, frequency = frequency density × class width
A criticism must name a fault in the method described, and the improvement must repair that fault
notOnThisSpec: Systematic, cluster, quota or multi-stage sampling as named techniques (M4-HD-01 names stratified sampling only)
Standard error, confidence intervals or any measure of sampling uncertainty (A level, not GCSE)
Random number tables and formal randomisation procedures

note.title: Stratified sampling and population estimates
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: Stratum share = (stratum size ÷ population) × sample size
Population estimate: marked in sample ÷ sample size = marked in population ÷ population
Part of a class = (part width ÷ class width) × frequency
Histogram: frequency = frequency density × class width

notOnThisSpec: Systematic, cluster or quota sampling by name
Confidence intervals or standard error (A level, not GCSE)

mustBeAbleTo: Work out how many from each group belong in a stratified sample, and check that the parts add to the sample size
Round a stratum share to a whole person, and decide which group takes an extra place when the rounded parts fall short
Work backwards: find the sample size, or a group's size in the population, from one group's contribution
Take a stratified sample from a subgroup named in the question, using that subgroup's total as the population
Estimate part of a class by proportion of its width, assuming an even spread
Read frequencies off a histogram (frequency density × class width) and then sample from them
Estimate a population from a marked sample and a recapture, giving a whole number of animals
Criticise the sampling method actually described, and give an improvement that repairs that fault
Decide, using the figures given, whether a sample represents a group fairly
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). One item most series, and it moves. A 3- to 4-mark stratified calculation, often the last part of a longer statistics question: Summer 2023 Q18 (complete the table, well answered), Summer 2025 Q22(c) (a sample of five from those waiting longer than six hours — many blank), November 2025 Q23(c) (a sample of 80 taken from frequencies that had to be read off a histogram), Summer 2026 Q20 (a sample of 20 from those above a threshold, 3 marks). Separately, a 4- to 5-mark population-estimate question with a written critique: Summer 2024 Q15, where 28% got full marks. Schemes read MA1 for the group total, MA1 for the proportion and A1 for the whole-number answer; in the critique each of the fault and the improvement is a separate A1.
traps: Writing the group's size in the population instead of its share of the sample (November 2025 M4 Q23)
Using the whole table's total when the sample is drawn from a subgroup only (Summer 2025 M4 Q22(c), where many left it blank)
Leaving a decimal number of people or animals on the answer line (Summer 2024 M4 Q15)
Turning the proportion upside down, so the population goes on top
Splitting the sample equally between the groups instead of proportionally
Giving a memorised critique — 'the sample is too small' — instead of a fault in the method described (Summer 2024 M4 Q15)
Listing principles of representativeness when the question hands you numbers to calculate with (Summer 2025 M4 Q18)
Adding bar heights on a histogram instead of multiplying each density by its class width (November 2025 M4 Q23)
Getting two of the three groups right and slipping on the third: add your group sizes back up and check they come to the sample size before you write them on the answer lines (Summer 2023 M4 Q18)

steps.working: Each group's share of the sample $=$ (group size $\div$ population) $\times$ sample size
steps.decision: Stratified means every group is represented in the same proportion as in the population. Writing the rule once, before any arithmetic, is what turns five calculations into one repeated calculation.

options: Because each group should be the same fraction of the sample as it is of the population
Because every group must contribute the same number of pupils
Because the sample must be the same size as the smallest group
whyMenu.explain: A stratified sample copies the shape of the population. Equal numbers from each group would over-represent the small groups.

steps.decision: The fraction is the group's share of the school; multiplying by 75 turns that share into pupils.
Same calculation, four more times. Keep the decimals visible for now — rounding before the check at the end can lose a pupil.

Pupils are whole people, so each figure is rounded to the nearest whole number. In Summer 2024 the examiners noted candidates who left a decimal number of animals in a population question; the same rule applies here.

options: Because you cannot put 16.2 pupils in a sample
Because the answer must always be even
Because decimals are not allowed in statistics
whyMenu.explain: The thing being counted is people, so the answer has to be a whole number of them.

steps.decision: Add the rounded figures and compare with the sample size. They come to 75, so nothing has to be adjusted. If they had come to 74 or 76, one group would be moved by one — the one whose decimal was closest to the halfway point.

workedExamples.stem:
24 trout were caught in a lake, marked and returned. Two weeks later 30 trout were caught, and 4 of them were marked.

(a) Estimate the number of trout in the lake.
(b) State one fault with this method and suggest one improvement.

steps.working: $\dfrac{\text{marked in the second sample}}{\text{size of the second sample}} = \dfrac{\text{marked in the lake}}{\text{trout in the lake}}$
steps.decision: The whole method is one assumption: the marked fish have mixed in, so the proportion marked in a handful is the proportion marked in the lake. Writing the two fractions is the method mark.

options: Because the marked fish are assumed to have spread evenly through the lake
Because the two samples were the same size
whyMenu.explain: Even mixing is what lets a small catch stand for the whole lake. If the marked fish stayed together, the second catch would tell you nothing about the rest.

steps.decision: Put the numbers in with the marked counts on top and the totals underneath, on both sides. In Summer 2024 only about a quarter of candidates got this far: most did not recognise the proportion argument.
Cross-multiply and divide. A quick sense check: 4 out of 30 is about one in seven, and 24 is about one seventh of 180.

steps.working: Fault: the marks may have worn off, or the trout may not have mixed back through the lake in two weeks. Improvement: use a tag that lasts, and leave longer between the two catches so the marked fish spread out.
steps.decision: The criticism has to be about **this** procedure. The Summer 2024 examiners said critiques were often generic — 'the sample is too small' — when the marks were for faults in the method described.

workedExamples.stem:
The table shows the time $t$, in minutes, that 150 customers waited to be served.

$0 < t \le 10$: 24; $10 < t \le 20$: 36; $20 < t \le 30$: 48; $30 < t \le 50$: 30; $50 < t \le 80$: 12.

A stratified sample of 30 customers is taken **from those who waited longer than 20 minutes**. Estimate how many customers in this sample waited between 25 and 40 minutes.

steps.working: Those who waited longer than 20 minutes: $48 + 30 + 12 = 90$
steps.decision: The sample is not taken from all 150. The first job is to find the population the sample actually comes from, and 150 must not appear again.

options: Because the sample is drawn only from the customers who waited over 20 minutes
Because 150 is too large a number to divide by
Because the first two rows are not needed for any part of the question
whyMenu.explain: The stem restricts the sample to a subgroup, so that subgroup is the population for this calculation. Using 150 gives an answer roughly half the right size.

steps.working: Between 25 and 30: half of the $20 < t \le 30$ class $= \tfrac{5}{10} \times 48 = 24$
steps.decision: 25 to 30 is 5 minutes out of the 10-minute class, so take that fraction of its frequency. This assumes the waits are spread evenly through the class, which is why the answer is an estimate.

steps.working: Between 30 and 40: $\tfrac{10}{20} \times 30 = 15$, so the group of interest is $24 + 15 = 39$
steps.decision: Same idea for the wider class: 10 minutes out of 20. Add the two pieces to get the number of customers we are sampling from.
Now the stratified rule, with the subgroup as the population. November 2025 examiners: of the candidates who had the frequencies right, many still did not scale them to the sample size.

twin.stem: Using the same table, a stratified sample of 45 customers is taken from those who waited longer than 10 minutes. Estimate how many in this sample waited between 15 and 35 minutes.

items.stem: A town has 4000 residents; 600 are aged over 70. A stratified sample of 200 residents is taken. How many should be over 70?
items.skill: Apply the stratified rule to one group

options.feedback: 600 ÷ 4000 × 200 = 30. The group is 15% of the town, so it is 15% of the sample.
That is the whole group in the town. A sample of 200 cannot contain 600 people; the group's count has to be scaled down to the sample.
The sample was split equally between groups. A stratified sample keeps each group's share, not equal shares.
The fraction was used upside down: 4000 ÷ 600 × 200. Group size goes on top, population underneath.

items.stem: A stratified sample of 50 is taken from 720 people. One group has 168 people. How many of them are in the sample?
items.skill: Round a stratum share to a whole person

options.feedback: 168 ÷ 720 × 50 = 11.67, and people are whole, so 12.
The arithmetic is right, but 11.67 people is not something you can sample. Round to the nearest whole person.
11.67 rounds up, not down. Round to the nearest whole number unless the question says otherwise.
That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of a sample of 50.

items.stem: 30 birds are caught, ringed and released. Later, 40 birds are caught and 5 are ringed. Which equation estimates the population $N$?

options.feedback: The proportion ringed in the second catch equals the proportion ringed in the whole population.
The fraction on the right is upside down. The ringed birds, 30, are the part; N is the whole.
Adding the two catches counts birds, not proportions, and gives a number far too small. The method compares fractions.
That has no connection to the 30 ringed birds. Every number in the stem has to appear in the proportion.

items.stem: A capture-recapture calculation gives $N = 146.67$. What should be written on the answer line?
items.skill: Give a population estimate as a whole number

options.feedback: Animals are whole, and the word 'estimate' in the question does not excuse a decimal.
The arithmetic is right but 0.67 of an animal cannot exist. The examiners named this loss in Summer 2024.
Rounding to 1 decimal place does not fix it: the unit is animals, so the answer is a whole number.
Rounding to 1 significant figure throws away accuracy the calculation earned. Round to the nearest whole animal.

items.stem: A table has 200 people in total. A stratified sample of 20 is taken **from the 80 people aged over 40**. Which total goes on the bottom of the fraction?
items.skill: Sample from a subgroup, not the whole table

options.feedback: The sample comes from that subgroup, so the subgroup is the population for this calculation.
The sample is not drawn from everyone. Using 200 makes every answer less than half the size it should be.
20 is the sample size, which multiplies the fraction; it is not the population.
That is the number aged 40 or under — the people the sample is not taken from.

items.stem: A class in a table is $20 < t \le 30$ with frequency 48. Estimate how many values lie between 25 and 30.

options.feedback: 25 to 30 is 5 of the 10 minutes, so take half the frequency, assuming an even spread.
That is the whole class, 20 to 30. Only the part above 25 is wanted.
5 is the width of the part in minutes, not a number of customers.
48 has been divided by 5 instead of multiplied by the fraction 5/10. Multiply the frequency by the share of the class you want.

items.stem: A survey of 200 people at a leisure centre contains 24 people aged over 65, although 22% of the town is over 65. Which comment would earn the reasoning mark?
items.skill: Argue from the numbers given, not from memorised points

options.text: 22% of 200 is 44, but only 24 were asked, so the over-65s are under-represented
options.feedback: The mark comes from doing the one calculation the data allows and comparing the two numbers.

options.text: The sample is too small to be representative
options.feedback: A memorised point with no use of the figures. Summer 2025 examiners said strong candidates lost this mark by listing principles instead of calculating.
This names a conclusion without evidence. Say which group is over- or under-represented and by how much.

options.text: 24 out of 200 is a small number of people
options.feedback: A comment on size rather than proportion. Compare 24 with the 44 the town's percentage would predict.

parts.stem: A gym has 500 members: 120 aged 16 to 25, 150 aged 26 to 35, 140 aged 36 to 50 and 90 aged 51 to 70. A stratified sample of 60 members is taken **from those aged 36 and over**. Estimate how many members in this sample are aged 51 to 70.

Add the two groups aged 36 and over first.
Round to a whole member.
parts.workedSolution: Members aged 36 and over: $140 + 90 = 230$. Then $\dfrac{90}{230} \times 60 = 23.48$, so 23 members.

context.setting: Masses of 240 parcels in a depot

parts.stem:
The table shows the mass $m$, in kg, of 240 parcels.

$0 < m \le 5$: 40; $5 < m \le 10$: 64; $10 < m \le 20$: 80; $20 < m \le 40$: 56.

A stratified sample of 44 parcels is taken from those with mass over 10 kg. Estimate how many parcels in this sample have a mass between 15 kg and 30 kg.
hints: First find how many parcels the sample is drawn from.
15 to 20 kg is half of the 10 to 20 class.
20 to 30 kg is half of the 20 to 40 class.
Then scale that total down to the sample of 44.
parts.workedSolution: Over 10 kg: $80 + 56 = 136$ parcels. Between 15 and 30 kg: $\tfrac{5}{10} \times 80 = 40$ and $\tfrac{10}{20} \times 56 = 28$, so $68$ parcels. Sample: $\dfrac{68}{136} \times 44 = 22$ parcels.

commonErrors.feedback: The total of the whole table was used underneath. The sample is drawn only from the subgroup named in the question, so that subgroup's total is the population here.
That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of the sample. Multiply the group's fraction by the sample size; the whole point of the method is to scale down.

context.setting: A survey carried out at one time and place

parts.stem: A researcher stands outside a supermarket between 10 am and 11 am on a Tuesday and asks the first 50 shoppers how often they buy fresh fish. State one fault with this sampling method and suggest one improvement.

accepted: Only people who shop on a weekday morning can be asked, so people at work are left out; ask at several different times and on different days
Everyone asked already shops at this supermarket, so it says nothing about shoppers elsewhere; survey at more than one shop

scheme.for: a fault tied to this method: one time of day, one day of the week, or one shop, so a whole group of shoppers cannot appear
an improvement that repairs the stated fault: survey at several times, on several days, or at more than one shop

hints: Ask yourself who could never be asked by this method.
The improvement must fix the fault you named, not just enlarge the sample.
parts.workedSolution: Fault: everyone asked is a weekday-morning shopper at one supermarket, so people who work during the day, or shop elsewhere, cannot be chosen. Improvement: repeat the survey at several different times and on different days, and at more than one shop.

commonErrors.feedback: This is the memorised answer, and it does not describe anything in the method given. Name the group this procedure can never reach, then say what would reach them.

questions.solutionProgram: No numeric answer: the two marks are one specific fault and one matching improvement

context.setting: A club sample tested for representativeness

parts.stem: A club has 180 members, of whom 45 are juniors. A sample of 60 members is taken, and 9 of them are juniors. Explain whether this sample represents the club's junior members fairly. Use the figures in your answer.

accepted: 45 out of 180 is 25%, and 25% of 60 is 15, but only 9 juniors were chosen, so juniors are under-represented

scheme.for: comparison stated: 9 is fewer than 15, so juniors are under-represented
scheme.examinerNote: A memorised comment about representativeness with no calculation scores nothing.

hints: Work out what fraction of the club is junior.
Apply that fraction to the sample of 60 to see how many juniors you would expect.
Compare that with the 9 actually chosen, and say which way it goes.
parts.workedSolution: Juniors are $\dfrac{45}{180} = 25\%$ of the club. A fair sample of 60 would contain $0.25 \times 60 = 15$ juniors, but only 9 were chosen, so juniors are under-represented in this sample.

commonErrors.feedback: The reasoning mark comes from the numbers in the question. Summer 2025 examiners said even strong candidates listed memorised points; those who did the one calculation the data allowed scored.

context.setting: Four year groups whose rounded shares do not add to the sample size

parts.stem: A college has 580 students: 186 in Year 11, 154 in Year 12, 132 in Year 13 and 108 in Year 14. A stratified sample of 50 students is taken. Work out the number from each year group, rounded to the nearest whole student.
hints: Group ÷ population × sample size, four times.
Keep two decimal places before rounding.
parts.workedSolution: The four unrounded shares are $16.03$, $13.28$, $11.38$, $9.31$, which round to 16, 13, 11, 9.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of the sample. Multiply the group's fraction by the sample size; the whole point of the method is to scale down.

parts.stem: Your four numbers do not add to 50. Explain which year group should provide the extra student, and why.

accepted: The four rounded numbers add to 49, so one more is needed; Year 13's unrounded value 11.38 was the furthest below a whole number, so Year 13 provides the extra student

scheme.for: Year 13 takes the extra student, because its unrounded value 11.38 had the largest fractional part and so was rounded down by the most

hints: Add your four rounded numbers and compare with 50.
Look back at the unrounded figures and find the one that lost the most in rounding.
parts.workedSolution: $16 + 13 + 11 + 9 = 49$, which is 1 short of the 50 required. The unrounded values were $16.03$, $13.28$, $11.38$, $9.31$; the largest fractional part is $0.38$ in Year 13, so that group provides the extra student and the sample is complete.

pattern.regex: leave it|does not matter|49 is fine

commonErrors.feedback: The sample must contain the number of students asked for. One group takes the extra place, and the fairest choice is the one whose exact share was cut back the most by rounding.

questions.solutionProgram: raw shares of 50 from 186/154/132/108 of 580 = 16.03, 13.28, 11.38, 9.31; rounded 16, 13, 11, 9 sum 49; shortfall 1; largest fractional part index 2

A sports club has 900 members: 180 under 12, 240 12 to 15, 150 16 to 18, 330 over 18.

A stratified sample of 60 members is to be taken. Complete the table to show how many members from each age group should be in the sample. Show your working out clearly.

scheme.for: 180 ÷ 900 × 60 (or any one group) seen as the method
the four entries checked against the sample size: they total 60

hints: Each group keeps its share: group ÷ 900 × 60.
180 out of 900 is one fifth.
Add your four answers — they must come to 60.

commonErrors.feedback: The 60 has been shared equally between the four groups. Stratified sampling keeps each group's proportion, so the 330-strong group must send far more than the 150-strong one.
The fraction is upside down. The group size goes on top and the population underneath, then multiply by the sample size.

context.setting: Marking and recapturing newts in a pond over two weeks

parts.stem:
A conservation group catches 45 newts in a pond, marks each one and returns it to the pond. Two weeks later they catch 60 newts, and 9 of them are marked.

Calculate an estimate of the number of newts in the pond.
hints: The fraction of the second catch that is marked should match the fraction of the pond that is marked.
9 out of 60 equals 45 out of N.
Give a whole number of newts.

commonErrors.feedback: The catches have been added rather than compared as proportions. Write the two fractions, marked over total on each side, and the method mark is secured even if the arithmetic slips.
The fraction is upside down. The group size goes on top and the population underneath, then multiply by the sample size.

parts.stem: State one fault with this method of estimating the population, and suggest how it could be improved.

accepted: The marks may wear off in two weeks, so marked newts are counted as unmarked; use a longer-lasting tag
Newts may have been born or died between the two catches; shorten the time between the catches
The marked newts may not have mixed back through the pond; leave longer, or catch from several places in the pond

scheme.for: a fault in the procedure described: marks wearing off, newts not mixing back, or births and deaths in the two weeks
an improvement that repairs the stated fault
reject: catch more newts (unless linked to a stated fault)

hints: What could change about the newts, or about the marks, in two weeks?
The improvement has to fix the fault you named.
parts.workedSolution: Fault: over two weeks the marks may fade, so a marked newt in the second catch is recorded as unmarked and the estimate comes out too large. Improvement: use a tag that will still be visible, and check the marks carefully before recording.

commonErrors.feedback: This is the point most candidates gave in Summer 2024, and it was not what the marks were for. The examiners wanted a criticism of the procedure described — marking, waiting, recatching.

parts.stem:
A library records the number of days $d$ that each of 300 books was on loan.

$0 < d \le 7$: 66; $7 < d \le 14$: 84; $14 < d \le 28$: 98; $28 < d \le 56$: 52.

A stratified sample of 50 books is taken from all 300. Estimate how many books in the sample were on loan for 14 days or less.

scheme.for: 66 + 84 = 150 books on loan for 14 days or less

hints: Add the first two classes.
The sample is taken from all 300 here.
150 out of 300 is half.
parts.workedSolution: Books on loan for 14 days or less: $66 + 84 = 150$. Sample: $\dfrac{150}{300} \times 50 = 25$ books.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of the sample. Multiply the group's fraction by the sample size; the whole point of the method is to scale down.

parts.stem: A second stratified sample, of 30 books, is taken from those on loan for more than 14 days. Estimate how many books in this second sample were on loan for between 21 and 42 days.

scheme.for: books on loan for more than 14 days = 98 + 52 = 150

hints: This sample comes only from the last two classes.
21 to 28 days is half of the 14 to 28 class.
28 to 42 days is half of the 28 to 56 class.
parts.workedSolution: More than 14 days: $98 + 52 = 150$ books. Between 21 and 42 days: $\tfrac{7}{14} \times 98 = 49$ and $\tfrac{14}{28} \times 52 = 26$, giving $75$. Sample: $\dfrac{75}{150} \times 30 = 15$ books.

commonErrors.feedback: The total of the whole table was used underneath. The sample is drawn only from the subgroup named in the question, so that subgroup's total is the population here.
That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of the sample. Multiply the group's fraction by the sample size; the whole point of the method is to scale down.

methodLock.instruction: Estimate how many books in this second sample
methodLock.requiredMethod: Subgroup total underneath the fraction, with each part-class found by proportion of its width; using the 300 total earns no accuracy mark

parts.stem:
The histogram below is about the heights of plants in a nursery.

Calculate how many plants it represents altogether.

scheme.for: frequency = frequency density × class width used for at least one bar

hints: The height of a bar is frequency density, not frequency.
Multiply each density by the width of its class.
The classes are not all the same width.

commonErrors.feedback: The bar heights have been added as if they were frequencies. On a histogram the area of a bar is the frequency, so multiply each height by its class width first.

parts.stem: A stratified sample of 44 plants is taken from the nursery. Estimate how many plants in the sample have a height of more than 50 cm.

scheme.for: plants over 50 cm: (10/20) × 40 = 20 and 20 from the last bar, total 40

hints: 50 cm falls in the middle of the 40 to 60 class.
Take the part of that bar above 50, then all of the last bar.
Scale the result down to the sample of 44.
parts.workedSolution: Above 50 cm: half of the 40 to 60 bar, $\tfrac{10}{20} \times 40 = 20$, plus all 20 of the 60 to 100 bar, giving $40$ plants. Sample: $\dfrac{40}{220} \times 44 = 8$ plants.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of the sample. Multiply the group's fraction by the sample size; the whole point of the method is to scale down.
Only the last bar was used. 50 cm cuts the 40 to 60 bar in half, so half of that bar's 40 plants belong in the group as well.

parts.stem: Give a reason why your answer to part (b) is only an estimate.

accepted: The individual heights inside each class are not known, so the plants are assumed to be spread evenly across the 40 to 60 class

scheme.for: the data is grouped, so splitting the 40 to 60 bar assumes the heights are spread evenly across the class

hints: What did you assume when you took half of the 40 to 60 bar?
parts.workedSolution: Because the histogram only records how many plants fall in each class, not their individual heights. Taking half of the 40 to 60 bar assumes the heights in that class are spread evenly, which may not be true.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeating the word in the question does not answer it. Name the assumption you made: that the heights are spread evenly inside the class you cut in half.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked: a village of 1200 people contains 320 people aged under 18. A stratified sample of 75 people is taken. How many should be under 18? Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The group's share of the village was worked out correctly and then the group's own size was written on the answer line. The share still has to be turned into people in the sample by multiplying by 75.
findTheMistake.feedback: The fraction is right and earns the method mark. The last step is the one that makes it a sample: multiply the fraction by the sample size. A sample of 75 cannot contain 320 people, and that check takes a second. November 2025 M4 Q23: of the candidates who had the frequencies right, many did not scale them to the sample size.

findTheMistake.stem: Finn was asked to estimate a rabbit population. 18 rabbits were caught, marked and released; later 28 rabbits were caught and 5 were marked. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Every line of the proportion and the arithmetic is correct. The answer line still reports 0.8 of a rabbit; a population is a whole number of animals.
findTheMistake.feedback: Both method marks stand: the proportion is set up exactly as the scheme wants and the calculation is right. Only the final accuracy mark is at risk, and one word — 'about 101 rabbits' — protects it. Summer 2024 M4 Q15: some candidates who found the estimate left a decimal number of animals and lost that mark.

findTheMistake.stem: Meabh was asked: a table shows 250 journeys, of which 60 took over 40 minutes and 40 took over 60 minutes. A stratified sample of 20 journeys is taken **from those over 40 minutes**. How many of the sample took over 60 minutes? Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The sample is drawn only from the 60 journeys over 40 minutes, so 60 is the population for this calculation, not 250. Using the whole table makes the answer far too small.
correction: The sample comes from the 60 journeys over 40 minutes
findTheMistake.feedback: The shape of the working is exactly right, which is worth noticing — the rule was applied correctly to the wrong population. Read the sampling sentence twice and underline the words that say where the sample comes from, then write that total down before anything else. Summer 2025 M4 Q22(c) asked for a sample from those waiting longer than six hours, and many left it blank.

prompts.prompt: How many from a group should appear in a stratified sample?
prompts.answer: $\dfrac{\text{group size}}{\text{population}} \times \text{sample size}$, rounded to a whole person.

prompts.prompt: What does stratified mean, and why is it used?
prompts.answer: Every group is represented in the sample in the same proportion as in the population, so no group is over- or under-represented. Equal numbers from each group would over-represent the small ones.

prompts.prompt: The capture-recapture relationship for estimating a population.
prompts.answer: $\dfrac{\text{marked in the second sample}}{\text{size of the second sample}} = \dfrac{\text{number marked}}{\text{population}}$, so population $= \dfrac{\text{marked} \times \text{second sample}}{\text{marked in it}}$.

prompts.prompt: A sample is taken **from those over 40 minutes**. Which total goes underneath the fraction?
prompts.answer: The total of that subgroup only, not the whole table. The restriction in the sentence redefines the population for that calculation.

prompts.prompt: Your stratified calculation gives 16.2 people. What goes on the answer line?
prompts.answer: 16 people. The thing being counted is people, so the answer is a whole number; a decimal costs the accuracy mark.

prompts.prompt: You have rounded four stratum shares and they add to 49 instead of 50. What now?
prompts.answer: Give the extra place to the group whose unrounded value had the largest fractional part, so the sample is the size asked for and the proportions stay as close as possible.

prompts.prompt: How do you estimate how many values in a class lie between two values inside it?
prompts.answer: Take the fraction of the class width you want and multiply by the frequency, assuming the values are spread evenly across the class. That assumption is why the answer is an estimate.

prompts.prompt: A question asks whether a sample represents a population, and gives numbers. What earns the mark?
prompts.answer: Doing the one calculation the numbers allow — work out the expected number from the population's proportion and compare it with the number in the sample. A memorised comment about representativeness earns nothing.

prompts.prompt: What makes a criticism of a sampling method worth a mark?
prompts.answer: It must name a fault in the procedure described — the time, the place, the method of marking, the gap between the catches — and the improvement must repair that fault. 'The sample is too small' is not tied to the method.

prompts.prompt: On a histogram, how do you get a frequency from a bar?
prompts.answer: Frequency = frequency density × class width, so the frequency is the **area** of the bar. Adding the bar heights counts nothing.

prompts.prompt: A group of 200 in a population of 1600 contributes how many to a stratified sample of 48?
80 fish are marked and released. Later 50 fish are caught and 6 are marked. Estimate the population, and say what you assumed.
prompts.answer: $\dfrac{6}{50} = \dfrac{80}{N}$, so $N = \dfrac{80 \times 50}{6} \approx 667$ fish. It assumes the marked fish mixed evenly back through the water and that none died or lost its mark.

findings.asked: Work out the numbers from each age group in a stratified sample.
findings.wentWrong: Mostly full marks; the rest were blank or wrong throughout, with the occasional slip in one age group only.
findings.rule: Group share of the sample = group size / population x sample size.

findings.asked: Estimate a population from a marked sample and a second sample, then give one fault and one improvement of the method.
findings.wentWrong: Only about a quarter got the estimate; most did not recognise the proportion argument. Some who did left a decimal number of animals. Critiques were often generic (sample size) rather than about the method described.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Set the proportion marked in the second sample equal to the proportion marked in the population, solved, and rounded to a whole number; then criticised the specific procedure in the question.
findings.rule: Marked in sample / sample size = marked in population / population; give whole animals and a fault tied to the given method.

findings.asked: Reason about whether a sample of a given size, with a given percentage, represents a population.
findings.wentWrong: Even strong candidates overthought it and listed memorised points about representativeness. Those who calculated 30% of 142 and compared it with the population got the marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Did the one calculation the data allowed and compared numbers, not principles.
findings.rule: When numbers are given, calculate with them; a reasoning mark comes from the specific data.

findings.asked: Stratified sample using frequencies read from a histogram.
findings.wentWrong: Only a small proportion finished; most had never got the frequencies right, and of those who had, many did not scale the group counts to the sample size.
findings.rule: Sample from a group = (group frequency / total) x sample size, rounded to a whole number.

insight.ruleToRemember: Stratified: each group gets the same fraction of the sample as it has of the population. Population estimate: proportion marked in the second sample = proportion marked in the population. Answers are whole people; criticisms must name the fault in the given method.
insight.aStarSignal: Doing the sampling calculation from frequencies that first had to be read off a histogram, and writing a data-specific reason rather than a memorised one.
